geometric-order-6c90b7c9.interpretation: The symbol $\rho$ denotes the background cosmic energy density, while $\delta \rho = \rho(\mathbf{x}, t) - \bar{\rho}(t)$ represents the local perturbation in density. geometric-order-6c90b7c9.symmetry_origin: Originates from the breaking of spatial translation and scale invariance during cosmological inflation, where quantum vacuum fluctuations of the inflaton field freeze out upon exiting the Hubble horizon.
geometric-order-6c90b7c9.limits_and_boundary: In the perfectly homogeneous limit $\delta \rho \to 0$, the spacetime reduces exactly to a Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) metric. geometric-order-6c90b7c9.conceptual_definition: The dimensionless ratio $\frac{\delta \rho}{\rho}$ characterizes the magnitude of primordial matter and energy density inhomogeneities relative to the background homogeneous cosmological density $\rho$. The measured value of order $10^{-5}$ represents the seed amplitude generated by quantum fluctuations during the inflationary epoch that eventually collapsed under gravity to form cosmic large-scale structure.
geometric-order-6c90b7c9.intuitive_summary: In the early universe, matter and radiation were nearly perfectly smooth, with tiny ripples of only one part in one hundred thousand that later grew into galaxies and clusters.
geometric-order-6c90b7c9.description: Quantifies the characteristic fractional density fluctuation amplitude imprinted in the early Universe during inflation, observed in the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) anisotropies.

thermodynamic-link-08404a7f.title: Ideal Gas Equation of State in Kinetic and Astrophysical Forms
thermodynamic-link-08404a7f.equation: P = nk_B T = \frac{\rho k_B T}{\mu m_H}

P.name: Thermodynamic Pressure
P.description: Kinetic gas pressure exerted on boundaries or adjacent fluid elements.

n.name: Particle Number Density
n.description: Total number of free particles (ions, electrons, neutral atoms) per unit volume.

k_B.name: Boltzmann Constant
k_B.description: Fundamental physical constant relating absolute temperature to microscopic particle kinetic energy.

T.name: Absolute Temperature
T.description: Thermodynamic temperature of the gas in thermal equilibrium.

\\rho.name: Mass Density
\\rho.description: Bulk mass per unit volume of the astrophysical fluid.

\\mu.name: Mean Molecular Weight
\\mu.description: Dimensionless average mass per particle in units of the hydrogen atom mass.

m_H.name: Hydrogen Atom Mass
m_H.description: Mass of a neutral hydrogen atom (or standard atomic mass unit reference).

thermodynamic-link-08404a7f.interpretation: The kinetic form $P = n k_B T$ directly connects pressure $P$ to the kinetic energy density of gas constituents, where $n$ represents the total number of free particles per unit volume. The astrophysical form replaces $n$ with $\frac{\rho}{\mu m_H}$, where $\rho$ is the bulk mass density and $\mu$ is the dimensionless mean molecular weight per particle. The product $\mu m_H$ represents the mean mass per free particle, making this relation versatile for fully ionized, partially ionized, or neutral multi-component stellar matter.
thermodynamic-link-08404a7f.symmetry_origin: Translational and rotational invariance of the Maxwell-Boltzmann phase-space distribution in momentum space under thermal equilibrium conditions.
thermodynamic-link-08404a7f.limits_and_boundary: Valid in the classical non-relativistic regime where thermal de Broglie wavelength is much smaller than interparticle spacing ($\lambda_{\text{th}} \ll n^{-1/3}$) and temperatures/densities are far from quantum degeneracy (Fermi-Dirac or Bose-Einstein) and extreme relativistic effects ($k_B T \ll m c^2$). As $\rho \to \infty$ at low $T$, quantum degeneracy pressure dominates.
thermodynamic-link-08404a7f.conceptual_definition: The ideal gas equation of state describes a system of non-interacting point particles in thermal equilibrium. In kinetic formulation, pressure is given by $P = n k_B T$, where $n$ is particle number density, $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant, and $T$ is temperature. In astrophysical fluid dynamics, this is expressed in terms of mass density $\rho$, mean molecular weight $\mu$, and the hydrogen atom mass $m_H$ as $P = \frac{\rho k_B T}{\mu m_H}$, setting the equivalence $n = \frac{\rho}{\mu m_H}$.
thermodynamic-link-08404a7f.intuitive_summary: Gas pressure represents the momentum transfer per unit area from thermal particle collisions; expressing it in terms of density and mean molecular weight accounts for varying chemical composition and ionization states in astrophysical plasmas.
thermodynamic-link-08404a7f.description: Relates the macroscopic thermodynamic pressure of a non-degenerate ideal gas to particle number density, temperature, and bulk mass density via the mean molecular weight.

weight-scaling-c856f365.title: Ultra-Relativistic Neutron Degeneracy Pressure

P_{rel}.name: Ultra-relativistic degeneracy pressure
P_{rel}.description: Outward pressure generated by degenerate fermions in the extreme relativistic regime.

\\hbar.name: Reduced Planck constant
\\hbar.description: Fundamental quantum of action governing phase-space cell volume.

c.name: Speed of light in vacuum
c.description: Universal constant setting the velocity scale in relativistic dispersion relations.

n_n.name: Neutron number density
n_n.description: Number of degenerate neutrons per unit volume.

weight-scaling-c856f365.interpretation: In this relation, $P_{\text{rel}}$ denotes the ultra-relativistic degeneracy pressure (in $\text{Pa}$). The prefactor $\frac{(3\pi^2)^{1/3}}{4}$ arises from phase-space integration over a spherical Fermi surface with spin degeneracy $g = 2$. The constant $\hbar$ is the reduced Planck constant ($\,\text{J}\cdot\text{s}$), $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum ($\text{m}/\text{s}$), and $n_n$ represents the neutron number density ($\text{m}^{-3}$). The $4/3$ power law signifies the softer relativistic equation of state compared to the $5/3$ non-relativistic scaling.
weight-scaling-c856f365.symmetry_origin: Spatial translation invariance leading to momentum conservation and global $U(1)$ fermion number conservation, combined with Fermi-Dirac antisymmetrization under the permutation group $S_N$.
weight-scaling-c856f365.limits_and_boundary: In the non-relativistic limit ($n_n \ll (m_n c / \hbar)^3$), the equation of state stiffens to $P \propto n_n^{5/3}$. In the classical limit $\hbar \to 0$, the degeneracy pressure vanishes ($P_{\text{rel}} \to 0$). At finite temperatures, thermal corrections enter as $\mathcal{O}((k_B T / E_F)^2)$ and are negligible when $T \ll T_F$.
weight-scaling-c856f365.conceptual_definition: In extreme density regimes where the Fermi momentum satisfies $p_F \gg m_n c$, the energy-momentum relation for degenerate neutrons becomes ultra-relativistic ($E \approx p c$). Integrating over the filled Fermi sphere in phase space yields an equation of state where pressure scales with the four-thirds power of the particle number density: $P_{\text{rel}} = \frac{(3\pi^2)^{1/3} \hbar c}{4} n_n^{4/3}$.
weight-scaling-c856f365.intuitive_summary: When neutrons are packed so densely that quantum confinement forces their speeds close to the speed of light, Pauli exclusion generates an outward quantum pressure proportional to $n_n^{4/3}$, independent of particle rest mass.
weight-scaling-c856f365.description: Calculates the degeneracy pressure exerted by a zero-temperature, ultra-relativistic Fermi gas of neutrons as a function of their number density.

stefan-boltzmann-relation-20394386.title: Stefan-Boltzmann Luminosity Relation for Spherical Radiators

stefan-boltzmann-relation-20394386.interpretation: In the relation $L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T_{\text{eff}}^4$, $L$ denotes the total radiant power or bolometric luminosity emitted across all wavelengths. The geometric factor $4\pi R^2$ represents the surface area of the spherical emitter of photospheric radius $R$. The constant $\sigma = \frac{2\pi^5 k_{\mathrm{B}}^4}{15 c^2 h^3}$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, representing the thermodynamic emission coupling for black bodies. The parameter $T_{\text{eff}}$ is the effective temperature, defined as the uniform temperature of an idealized black body that yields the equivalent emergent surface flux.
stefan-boltzmann-relation-20394386.symmetry_origin: Rotational $SO(3)$ spherical symmetry of the emitter and thermodynamic equilibrium of isotropic Planckian radiation fields governed by Lorentz and scale invariance.
stefan-boltzmann-relation-20394386.limits_and_boundary: As $T_{\text{eff}} \to 0$, $L \to 0$ in accordance with the third law of thermodynamics. In the point-source limit $R \to 0$, $L \to 0$. For real non-blackbody stellar atmospheres, deviation from an ideal Planckian spectrum is absorbed entirely into the operational definition of effective temperature $T_{\text{eff}}$.
stefan-boltzmann-relation-20394386.conceptual_definition: The Stefan-Boltzmann relation for a spherical emitter couples geometric surface integration over a sphere of radius $R$ with the integrated black-body flux density given by the Stefan-Boltzmann law $F = \sigma T_{\text{eff}}^4$. The total emitted power, or luminosity $L$, is the integral of the radiant flux over the spherical surface area $A = 4\pi R^2$, yielding $L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T_{\text{eff}}^4$.
stefan-boltzmann-relation-20394386.intuitive_summary: A star's total brightness is determined entirely by how large it is and how hot its surface is, scaling with surface area and exceptionally steeply with the fourth power of temperature.
stefan-boltzmann-relation-20394386.description: Relates the total bolometric luminosity emitted by a spherical black-body radiator, such as a star, to its radius and effective surface temperature.

free-streaming-322fac8a.title: Free-Streaming Length for eV-Scale Hot Dark Matter

\\lambda_{fs}.name: Free-streaming length
\\lambda_{fs}.description: The characteristic distance a particle travels while relativistic, setting the minimum scale for structure formation.

m_\\nu.name: Hot Dark Matter particle mass
m_\\nu.description: The mass of the hot dark matter particle, typically a massive neutrino.

\\text{Mpc}.name: Megaparsec
\\text{Mpc}.description: A unit of distance used in cosmology, equal to one million parsecs or approximately 3.26 million light-years.

\\text{eV}.name: Electron Volt
\\text{eV}.description: A unit of energy, commonly used in particle physics as a unit of mass via E=mc^2.

free-streaming-322fac8a.interpretation:
The formula $\lambda_{fs} \approx 20 	ext{ Mpc} / (m_
u / 30 	ext{ eV})$ establishes a numerical relationship for the free-streaming length, $\lambda_{fs}$, of a hot dark matter particle candidate, typically a massive neutrino. The length $\lambda_{fs}$ is inversely proportional to the particle's mass, $m_
u$. The constants are chosen for convenience: a hypothetical particle with a mass $m_
u = 30 	ext{ eV}$ would have a free-streaming length of approximately $20$ Megaparsecs (Mpc). This scale is cosmologically significant, as it implies that any structure smaller than $\lambda_{fs}$ would be suppressed by the particle's motion in the early universe. For a more realistic light neutrino mass of, say, $m_
u \sim 0.1 	ext{ eV}$, the free-streaming length would be enormous ($\sim 6000$ Mpc), which is inconsistent with observed small-scale structures.
free-streaming-322fac8a.symmetry_origin: This relation is not derived from a fundamental symmetry but is a phenomenological result emerging from the application of the Boltzmann equation to a particle distribution function within the framework of an expanding Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) spacetime, governed by General Relativity.
free-streaming-322fac8a.limits_and_boundary: In the limit of zero mass, $m_\nu \to 0$, the particle remains relativistic indefinitely, causing the free-streaming length to diverge, $\lambda_{fs} \to \infty$, erasing structure on all scales. Conversely, in the limit of very large mass, $m_\nu \to \infty$, the particle becomes non-relativistic very early, and the free-streaming length approaches zero, $\lambda_{fs} \to 0$. This is the Cold Dark Matter (CDM) limit, where structure formation is not suppressed by this mechanism. The formula is an approximation valid for particles that become non-relativistic around the epoch of matter-radiation equality.
free-streaming-322fac8a.conceptual_definition: Free-streaming is the process in the early universe where relativistic particles, such as hot dark matter (HDM), travel unimpeded from regions of high density to regions of low density. This movement erases density perturbations on scales smaller than the characteristic distance they can travel, known as the free-streaming length, $\lambda_{fs}$. This equation provides a convenient approximation for $\lambda_{fs}$ for particles with mass $m_\nu$ in the electron-volt (eV) range.
free-streaming-322fac8a.intuitive_summary: Imagine spraying a fine mist (hot dark matter particles) onto a dusty surface (primordial density fluctuations). The fast-moving mist droplets will blur out any small, detailed patterns in the dust, leaving only the large-scale patterns intact. The free-streaming length is the size of the smallest pattern that can survive this blurring effect. Lighter, faster particles create more blurring and have a larger free-streaming length.
free-streaming-322fac8a.description: Provides a numerical approximation for the free-streaming length of hot dark matter (HDM) particles, which determines the minimum scale for cosmic structure formation.

lorentz-cap-a0acc054.title: Spin-Orbit Interaction Energy Shift

\\Delta E_{SO}.name: Spin-orbit energy shift
\\Delta E_{SO}.description: Perturbative energy shift due to spin-orbit coupling

r.name: Radial distance

\\mathbf{L}.name: Orbital angular momentum operator
\\mathbf{L}.description: Vector operator of the electron's orbital angular momentum

\\mathbf{S}.name: Spin angular momentum operator
\\mathbf{S}.description: Vector operator of the electron's intrinsic spin angular momentum

lorentz-cap-a0acc054.interpretation: The term $\Delta E_{SO}$ represents the energy eigenvalue shift due to spin-orbit coupling. The radial coordinate $r$ measures the distance from the central nucleus, and $\frac{dV}{dr}$ is the radial derivative of the central electrostatic potential $V(r)$, defining the radial electric field $E_r = -\frac{dV}{dr}$. The orbital angular momentum vector is denoted by $\mathbf{L}$, while $\mathbf{S}$ denotes the spin angular momentum vector. The scalar product $\mathbf{L} \cdot \mathbf{S} = \frac{1}{2}(J(J+1) - L(L+1) - S(S+1))\hbar^2$ splits degenerate energy levels according to total angular momentum $J$.
lorentz-cap-a0acc054.symmetry_origin: Originates from the Lorentz covariance of relativistic quantum mechanics (Dirac equation) and breaks individual spatial rotational symmetry $SO(3)_L$ and spin rotational symmetry $SU(2)_S$, conserving only the coupled total angular momentum symmetry $SU(2)_J$.
lorentz-cap-a0acc054.limits_and_boundary: In the non-relativistic limit ($c \to \infty$), the fine-structure coupling constant vanishes and $\Delta E_{SO} \to 0$. As $r \to \infty$ in a Coulomb potential where $V(r) \propto -1/r$, the energy correction falls off asymptotically as $r^{-3}$. For $S$-states ($L=0$), the expectation value $\langle \mathbf{L} \cdot \mathbf{S} \rangle$ vanishes identically.
lorentz-cap-a0acc054.conceptual_definition: The spin-orbit coupling energy shift $\Delta E_{SO}$ is a relativistic fine-structure correction given by $\Delta E_{SO} \propto \frac{1}{r} \frac{dV}{dr} \mathbf{L} \cdot \mathbf{S}$, where the moving electron experiences an effective magnetic field $\mathbf{B} = -\frac{\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{E}}{c^2}$ proportional to the radial electric field gradient $\frac{1}{r}\frac{dV}{dr}$, which couples to its intrinsic spin magnetic dipole moment $\boldsymbol{\mu}_S$ with an additional Thomas precession factor of $\frac{1}{2}$.
lorentz-cap-a0acc054.intuitive_summary: In the rest frame of an orbiting electron, the charged nucleus appears to revolve around it, creating an effective magnetic field that aligns or anti-aligns with the electron's intrinsic spin.
lorentz-cap-a0acc054.description: Quantifies the perturbative energy shift in atomic systems arising from the relativistic coupling between the electron's spin magnetic dipole moment and the internal magnetic field induced by its orbital motion through the central electrostatic potential.

functional-reduction-e7fdac48.title: Wilsonian Effective Action via Functional Reduction

S_{eff}[\\phi_{light}].name: effective action
S_{eff}[\\phi_{light}].description: Wilsonian effective action functional governing the low-energy dynamics of the light fields

\\phi_{light}.name: light field configuration
\\phi_{light}.description: Background or propagating field degree of freedom with mass or energy below the integration cutoff

\\mathcal{D}\\phi_{heavy}.name: functional integration measure
\\mathcal{D}\\phi_{heavy}.description: Path integral measure over all field configurations of the heavy degrees of freedom

\\phi_{heavy}.description: Massive or high-frequency field degree of freedom integrated out from the low-energy theory

S[\\phi_{light}, \\phi_{heavy}].name: full microscopic action functional

functional-reduction-e7fdac48.interpretation: The left-hand side $e^{i S_{\text{eff}}[\phi_{\text{light}}]}$ represents the quantum amplitude governed purely by the light fields $\phi_{\text{light}}$ through their effective action $S_{\text{eff}}$. On the right-hand side, $\int \mathcal{D}\phi_{\text{heavy}}$ denotes functional integration over the full configuration space of heavy fields $\phi_{\text{heavy}}$, with the integrand being the phase factor generated by the microscopic bare action $S[\phi_{\text{light}}, \phi_{\text{heavy}}]$ in natural units where $\hbar = 1$.
functional-reduction-e7fdac48.symmetry_origin: Maintains invariance under global and unbroken gauge symmetries shared by the microscopic theory, reflecting the semigroup property of the Wilsonian Renormalization Group flow.
functional-reduction-e7fdac48.limits_and_boundary: In the infinite heavy mass limit $M_{\text{heavy}} \to \infty$, the Appelquist-Carazzone decoupling theorem guarantees that heavy fields decouple, yielding local operator corrections suppressed by inverse powers of $M_{\text{heavy}}$. In the classical limit $\hbar \to 0$, the path integral reduces via the stationary-phase approximation to evaluating the microscopic action at the classical equation of motion for $\phi_{\text{heavy}}(\phi_{\text{light}})$.
functional-reduction-e7fdac48.conceptual_definition: In quantum field theory and the Wilsonian renormalization group framework, the effective action $S_{\text{eff}}[\phi_{\text{light}}]$ encapsulates all quantum dynamics of the light degrees of freedom $\phi_{\text{light}}$ below a characteristic energy scale $M$. It is formally defined by evaluating the path integral over the complementary heavy degrees of freedom $\phi_{\text{heavy}}$, effectively mapping the full high-energy action $S[\phi_{\text{light}}, \phi_{\text{heavy}}]$ to a non-local or derivative-expanded effective action for the light fields alone.
functional-reduction-e7fdac48.intuitive_summary: Integrating out heavy degrees of freedom accounts for virtual fluctuations of massive particles, replacing their explicit propagation with modified coupling constants and higher-dimensional contact operators among the remaining light particles.
functional-reduction-e7fdac48.description: Defines the low-energy effective action obtained by functionally integrating out high-energy or heavy field degrees of freedom in the path integral.

locality-a7ecd4b4.title: Quantum Non-Locality and Failure of Local Deterministic Realism

\\theta_{\\text{particle}}.name: particle state or observable parameter
\\theta_{\\text{particle}}.description: Instantaneous quantum property, state parameter, or measurement outcome associated with the particle

f.name: deterministic mapping function
f.description: Deterministic causal function operating on local historical data

\\text{Past Information}.name: local historical state set
\\text{Past Information}.description: Complete collection of classical events, local interactions, and parameters residing in the particle's backward light cone

locality-a7ecd4b4.interpretation: In this relation, $\theta_{\text{particle}}$ represents an observable property, quantum state parameter, or measurement outcome of a particle. The function $f$ represents any deterministic, classical mapping operating exclusively on the domain $\text{Past Information}$, which denotes the set of local historical interactions, classical trajectories, and local parameters within the particle's backward light cone. The strict inequality $\neq$ encapsulates the non-reducibility of quantum measurement statistics to local classical causal histories, directly reflecting phenomena such as quantum entanglement and the violation of local factorizability.
locality-a7ecd4b4.symmetry_origin: Relativistic causality and Lorentz invariance constrain information propagation within the light cone, whereas the non-local structure of quantum Hilbert spaces breaks classical local factorizability without violating relativistic microcausality.
locality-a7ecd4b4.limits_and_boundary: In the classical limit $\hbar \to 0$, quantum entanglement decoheres into classical statistical mixtures, and the state evolution satisfies local determinism such that $\theta_{\text{particle}} \to f(\mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{p}_0, t)$. In the fully entangled regime ($S > 2$ in the CHSH inequality), non-local correlations maximize up to Tsirelson's bound.
locality-a7ecd4b4.conceptual_definition: The inequality $\theta_{\text{particle}} \neq f(\text{Past Information})$ represents the breakdown of local hidden-variable determinism in quantum mechanics, as demonstrated by Bell's theorem and quantum entanglement. It asserts that the physical observable or state $\theta_{\text{particle}}$ is not strictly predictable from the local historical trajectory and classical past information of the isolated particle due to non-local quantum correlations and the probabilistic nature of quantum measurement.
locality-a7ecd4b4.intuitive_summary: A particle's quantum properties cannot be completely explained by where it has been or what happened to it locally in the past; entangled connections across space defy local classical history.
locality-a7ecd4b4.description: Formal symbolic expression denoting that the instantaneous quantum state or measurement outcome $\theta_{\text{particle}}$ cannot be determined as a local, single-particle deterministic function $f$ solely dependent on its past light-cone history.

invariant-interval-identity-3cf85959.title: Invariant Interval Identity

ds^2.name: Invariant Interval Squared
ds^2.description: The square of the spacetime interval between two events. It is invariant under Lorentz transformations, meaning all inertial observers will measure the same value for ds^2 for the same pair of events.

c.name: Speed of Light in Vacuum
c.description: The fundamental constant representing the speed of light in a vacuum, approximately $299,792,458$ m/s. It acts as a conversion factor between time and space in relativistic physics.

dt.name: Time Interval
dt.description: The time difference between two events as measured by an observer in a specific inertial frame of reference.

dx.name: Spatial Interval along x-axis
dx.description: The difference in the x-coordinate between two events in a specific inertial frame of reference.

dy.name: Spatial Interval along y-axis
dy.description: The difference in the y-coordinate between two events in a specific inertial frame of reference.

dz.name: Spatial Interval along z-axis
dz.description: The difference in the z-coordinate between two events in a specific inertial frame of reference.

s.description: The SI unit of time, or the invariant interval traversed by a clock.

z.description: A coordinate representing the longitudinal or altitude location of a particle in space.

invariant-interval-identity-3cf85959.interpretation: The equation defines the invariant interval squared, denoted as $ds^2$, which is a measure of the separation between two events in spacetime. The term $c^2 dt^2$ represents the contribution from the time separation, where $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum (a constant, approximately $299,792,458$ m/s) and $dt$ is the time elapsed between the two events in a given inertial frame. The term $dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2$ represents the contribution from the spatial separation between the events, where $dx$, $dy$, and $dz$ are the differences in the spatial coordinates (in meters) between the two events. The Minkowski metric, indicated by the negative sign before the spatial terms, is crucial: it signifies that time and space have different 'signs' in the structure of spacetime. If $ds^2 > 0$, the interval is called 'timelike,' meaning one event can causally influence the other. If $ds^2 < 0$, the interval is 'spacelike,' and the events cannot influence each other. If $ds^2 = 0$, the interval is 'lightlike' or 'null,' indicating that the two events are separated by a distance light can travel in the time between them.
invariant-interval-identity-3cf85959.symmetry_origin: The Invariant Interval Identity originates from the postulates of special relativity, particularly the constancy of the speed of light for all inertial observers. Lorentz transformations, which relate measurements between different inertial frames, preserve this spacetime interval. This invariance is a direct consequence of the Minkowski spacetime geometry, where the metric tensor effectively defines the invariant 'distance' in a four-dimensional pseudo-Euclidean space.
invariant-interval-identity-3cf85959.limits_and_boundary: As the spatial separation $dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2$ approaches zero, the interval becomes dominated by the temporal separation $c^2 dt^2$, and $ds^2 \approx c^2 dt^2$. In this limit, the events are separated only in time, and the interval is timelike. Conversely, as the temporal separation $dt$ approaches zero, the interval is dominated by the spatial separation $dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2$, and $ds^2 \approx -(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2)$. In this limit, the events are simultaneous in some frame and separated only in space, and the interval is spacelike. The boundary case $ds^2 = 0$ represents events connected by a light ray.
invariant-interval-identity-3cf85959.conceptual_definition: The Invariant Interval Identity, also known as the spacetime interval or Minkowski interval, is a fundamental concept in Einstein's theory of special relativity. It quantifies the 'distance' between two events in spacetime. Unlike spatial distances or time intervals, which are relative and depend on the observer's inertial frame of reference, the spacetime interval is invariant – it has the same value for all inertial observers. This invariance is a cornerstone of special relativity, reflecting the underlying structure of spacetime.
invariant-interval-identity-3cf85959.intuitive_summary: The spacetime interval squared is a conserved measure of 'spacetime separation' between two events, independent of the observer's motion.

coarse-grained-density-cb6a046e.title: Coarse-Grained Phase-Space Probability Density

\\bar{\\rho}.name: Coarse-grained phase-space density
\\bar{\\rho}.description: Averaged probability density assigned to a macroscopic phase-space volume element

P.name: Macroscopic momentum coordinates
P.description: Representative generalized momentum coordinates of the coarse-graining cell

Q.name: Macroscopic position coordinates
Q.description: Representative generalized position coordinates of the coarse-graining cell

\\Delta\\Gamma.name: Phase-space cell volume
\\Delta\\Gamma.description: Measure of the finite region in $6N$-dimensional phase space over which averaging is performed

\\rho.name: Fine-grained phase-space density
\\rho.description: Exact microscopic probability distribution function obeying the Liouville equation

p.name: Microscopic generalized momenta
p.description: Microscopic canonical momentum variables of all particles

q.name: Microscopic generalized coordinates
q.description: Microscopic canonical position variables of all particles

d\\Gamma.name: Phase-space volume differential
d\\Gamma.description: Differential volume element in $6N$-dimensional canonical phase space, given by $d^{3N}p\,d^{3N}q$

coarse-grained-density-cb6a046e.interpretation: The quantity $\bar{\rho}(P, Q)$ represents the coarse-grained probability density associated with a finite macro-cell centered at canonical phase-space coordinates $(P, Q)$. The integral $\int_{\Delta\Gamma} \rho(p, q) \, d\Gamma$ integrates the exact, fine-grained microscopic probability density $\rho(p, q)$ over the cell domain $\Delta\Gamma$. The prefactor $\frac{1}{\Delta\Gamma}$ normalizes this integral by the canonical phase-space volume measure of the cell $\Delta\Gamma = \int_{\Delta\Gamma} d^{3N}p \, d^{3N}q$, yielding a piecewise constant or smoothed local spatial-momentum probability measure.
coarse-grained-density-cb6a046e.symmetry_origin: Rooted in canonical invariance and symplectic geometry of Hamiltonian phase space, where the volume element $d\Gamma = \prod_{i=1}^{3N} dq_i \wedge dp_i$ is preserved under canonical transformations by Liouville's theorem.
coarse-grained-density-cb6a046e.limits_and_boundary: In the continuum limit $\Delta\Gamma \to 0$, the coarse-grained density converges point-wise to the microscopic fine-grained density: $\lim_{\Delta\Gamma \to 0} \bar{\rho}(P, Q) = \rho(p, q)$. In the macroscopic limit where $\Delta\Gamma$ spans the accessible energy shell $\Gamma_E$, $\bar{\rho}$ reduces to the uniform microcanonical ensemble density $\bar{\rho} = 1/\Omega(E)$. In quantum statistical mechanics, the minimal coarse-graining volume is bounded from below by the uncertainty principle, $\Delta\Gamma \ge h^{3N}$.
coarse-grained-density-cb6a046e.conceptual_definition: In non-equilibrium statistical mechanics and ergodic theory, coarse-graining represents the macroscopic observation process where microscopic details below a resolution scale $\Delta\Gamma$ are inaccessible. The coarse-grained density $\bar{\rho}(P, Q)$ assigns to an entire phase-space cell $\Delta\Gamma$ centered around macroscopic coordinates $(P, Q)$ the arithmetic mean of the fine-grained Gibbsian distribution $\rho(p, q)$. This mathematical operation breaks the time-reversal invariance of the exact microscopic Liouville dynamics and provides the foundational mechanism for the monotonic increase of coarse-grained Gibbs entropy ($S_{\mathrm{CG}} = -k_B \int \bar{\rho} \ln \bar{\rho} \, d\Gamma$), resolving the Gibbs paradox regarding entropy conservation in Hamiltonian systems.
coarse-grained-density-cb6a046e.intuitive_summary: Microscopic particles move precisely according to deterministic mechanics, keeping the fine-grained phase-space density constant along trajectories (Liouville's theorem). However, realistic measurements cannot resolve infinitely fine phase-space filaments. By averaging the distribution over small finite boxes (coarse-graining), the distribution smooths out, capturing macroscopic irreversibility and the emergence of thermodynamic entropy.
coarse-grained-density-cb6a046e.description: Defines the coarse-grained probability distribution function in statistical mechanics by averaging the microscopic fine-grained phase-space density over finite phase-space cells of volume $\Delta\Gamma$.

bayesian-updating-for-realism-aa5762cf.title: Bayesian Updating for Scientific Theory Realism

P(\\text{Theory}|\\text{Success}).name: Posterior probability of the theory
P(\\text{Theory}|\\text{Success}).description: The probability that the theory is true given the observed empirical success.

P(\\text{Success}|\\text{Theory}).name: Likelihood of success
P(\\text{Success}|\\text{Theory}).description: The conditional probability of obtaining the observed experimental success assuming the theory is true.

P(\\text{Theory}).name: Prior probability of the theory
P(\\text{Theory}).description: The initial subjective or objective degree of belief in the theory prior to the new evidence.

P(\\text{Success}).name: Marginal likelihood of success
P(\\text{Success}).description: The total integrated probability of observing the success across all possible theoretical models.

bayesian-updating-for-realism-aa5762cf.interpretation: In this formula, $P(\text{Theory}|\text{Success})$ represents the posterior probability of the theory being true after observing empirical success. The term $P(\text{Success}|\text{Theory})$ is the likelihood of observing the specific experimental success under the assumption that the theory holds. The prior probability $P(\text{Theory})$ encodes initial plausibility before novel evidence is integrated. The denominator $P(\text{Success})$ is the marginal probability of observing the success across the hypothesis space, functioning as the Bayesian evidence normalization factor.
bayesian-updating-for-realism-aa5762cf.symmetry_origin: Rooted in Kolmogorov probability axioms, Cox's theorem of consistent plausibility reasoning, and the normalization of probability measures over hypothesis spaces.
bayesian-updating-for-realism-aa5762cf.limits_and_boundary: As $P(\text{Theory}) \to 0$, $P(\text{Theory}|\text{Success}) \to 0$ (no amount of evidence revives an impossible prior). As $P(\text{Success}|\text{Theory}) \to 1$ while $P(\text{Success}|\neg\text{Theory}) \to 0$, $P(\text{Theory}|\text{Success}) \to 1$ (maximally distinctive novel predictive success implies certainty in realism).
bayesian-updating-for-realism-aa5762cf.conceptual_definition: The Bayesian formulation of scientific realism models the credibility of a theoretical framework as a conditional probability distribution. Given empirical verification or predictive success, the posterior probability $P(\text{Theory}|\text{Success})$ is obtained by scaling the prior degree of belief $P(\text{Theory})$ by the likelihood $P(\text{Success}|\text{Theory})$ relative to the marginal probability of that empirical success $P(\text{Success})$.
bayesian-updating-for-realism-aa5762cf.intuitive_summary: Observing successful experimental outcomes increases confidence in a scientific theory proportionally to how uniquely and accurately the theory predicted those outcomes compared to all alternative explanations.
bayesian-updating-for-realism-aa5762cf.description: Applies Bayes' theorem to scientific epistemology to calculate the posterior probability of a theory's truth conditional on empirical success.

b-minus-l-to-baryon-conversion-ratio-24f.title: Baryon Asymmetry from B-L Conversion (Electroweak Sphalerons)
b-minus-l-to-baryon-conversion-ratio-24f.interpretation: The formula $Y_B = \frac{28}{79} Y_{B-L}$ relates the final baryon asymmetry to a pre-existing $B-L$ asymmetry. The term $Y_B$ is the baryon yield, defined as the ratio of the net baryon number density to the entropy density, $Y_B = (n_B - n_{\bar{B}})/s$. It quantifies the baryon asymmetry in a comoving volume. The term $Y_{B-L}$ is the corresponding yield for the $B-L$ number, $Y_{B-L} = (n_{B} - n_{L})/s$. This quantity is assumed to be generated by physics beyond the Standard Model and is conserved by electroweak sphalerons. The constant factor $\frac{28}{79}$ is a thermal equilibrium coefficient derived from statistical mechanics, reflecting how the initial $B-L$ chemical potential is distributed among the chemical potentials of all Standard Model fermions (3 generations of quarks and leptons) by the sphaleron process, which enforces a relationship between them.
b-minus-l-to-baryon-conversion-ratio-24f.symmetry_origin: This relationship arises from the violation of baryon ($B$) and lepton ($L$) number symmetries due to the chiral anomaly in the electroweak sector of the Standard Model. However, the combination $B-L$ remains an accidentally conserved global symmetry in the Standard Model, even in the presence of these non-perturbative sphaleron effects. The formula describes the consequence of $B$ and $L$ violation under the constraint of $B-L$ conservation.
b-minus-l-to-baryon-conversion-ratio-24f.limits_and_boundary: This formula is valid for temperatures $T$ below the scale where the initial $B-L$ asymmetry is generated, but above the electroweak phase transition temperature ($T > T_{EW} \approx 100$ GeV), where sphalerons are active and unsuppressed. For temperatures $T \ll T_{EW}$, sphaleron processes become exponentially suppressed, and the baryon number $Y_B$ 'freezes out,' becoming a fixed relic abundance. If the initial $B-L$ asymmetry is zero ($Y_{B-L} = 0$), then no baryon asymmetry is generated through this mechanism, resulting in $Y_B = 0$.

b-minus-l-to-baryon-conversion-ratio-24f.conceptual_definition: In the early universe, at temperatures above the electroweak scale ($T > T_{EW} \approx 100$ GeV), non-perturbative processes known as sphalerons are active. These processes violate baryon ($B$) and lepton ($L$) number individually but conserve their difference, $B-L$. If a net $B-L$ asymmetry, represented by the yield $Y_{B-L}$, is generated by some high-scale physics (e.g., leptogenesis), sphalerons will redistribute this asymmetry among all quarks and leptons in thermal equilibrium. This redistribution results in a net baryon asymmetry, with a yield $Y_B$, that is directly proportional to the initial $Y_{B-L}$. The proportionality constant, $\frac{28}{79}$, is determined by the number of active fermionic degrees of freedom in the Standard Model at that epoch.
b-minus-l-to-baryon-conversion-ratio-24f.intuitive_summary: Imagine a conserved quantity, 'red-minus-blue charge,' in a system with many types of particles. A special process can't create or destroy this net charge, but it can freely convert red particles into blue ones and vice-versa. If you start with an excess of 'red-minus-blue charge' (analogous to $B-L$), this process will spread it out among all available particle types, creating a net excess of both red particles (baryons) and blue particles (leptons) in a specific, fixed ratio determined by the particle census.
b-minus-l-to-baryon-conversion-ratio-24f.description: This equation quantifies how a primordial asymmetry in the conserved B-L (Baryon minus Lepton) number is converted into the observed baryon asymmetry of the universe by non-perturbative electroweak sphaleron processes.

compressible-bernoulli-enthalpy-ident-a5.title: Bernoulli Constant (Compressible)
compressible-bernoulli-enthalpy-ident-a5.interpretation: This equation is the Bernoulli principle extended to compressible flows. Each term represents energy per unit mass (a 'specific' energy). The term $\frac{1}{2}v^2$ is the specific kinetic energy. The term $gz$ is the specific potential energy due to gravity. The crucial term for compressible flow is the specific enthalpy, $h$, defined as $h = u + P/\rho$, where $u$ is the specific internal energy, $P$ is the pressure, and $\rho$ is the density. Enthalpy accounts for both the internal thermal energy of the fluid ($u$) and the 'flow work' ($P/\rho$) done by the fluid to maintain its pressure in the flow. The constancy of this sum along a streamline is a direct consequence of the first law of thermodynamics applied to a fluid element under steady, frictionless, and adiabatic conditions.
compressible-bernoulli-enthalpy-ident-a5.symmetry_origin: This equation is an integral form of the Euler equations of fluid motion, which express conservation of momentum. When combined with the conservation of mass and the first law of thermodynamics under the assumption of steady flow (time-invariance), it yields this conserved quantity along a streamline. The underlying symmetry is time-translation invariance of the system's governing laws, which, by Noether's theorem, leads to the conservation of energy.
compressible-bernoulli-enthalpy-ident-a5.limits_and_boundary:
1. Incompressible Limit: If the fluid density $\rho$ is assumed to be constant, and specific internal energy $u$ is also constant, the specific enthalpy $h$ can be written as $u_{const} + P/\rho$. The constant $u_{const}$ can be absorbed into the Bernoulli constant, and the equation reduces to the familiar incompressible form: $\frac{1}{2}v^2 + P/\rho + gz = \mathrm{constant}$.
2. Ideal Gas Limit: For a calorically perfect gas, specific enthalpy is given by $h = c_p T$, where $c_p$ is the specific heat capacity at constant pressure and $T$ is the absolute temperature. The equation becomes $\frac{1}{2}v^2 + c_p T + gz = \mathrm{constant}$, a form widely used in gas dynamics and aerodynamics.
3. Stagnation Point: At a point in the flow where the velocity $v$ is zero (a stagnation point), the kinetic energy is converted into enthalpy. This defines the stagnation enthalpy, $h_0 = h + \frac{1}{2}v^2$, which is constant throughout an adiabatic, inviscid flow field (not just along a streamline).

This is a statement of the conservation of energy per unit mass for the fluid.
compressible-bernoulli-enthalpy-ident-a5.intuitive_summary: For a steady, ideal compressible fluid, the total energy per unit mass—comprising kinetic, potential, and thermal (enthalpy) contributions—is conserved along its path.

multiplicity-identity-1-7bea30c9-053f9c2.title: Einstein Solid Multiplicity
multiplicity-identity-1-7bea30c9-053f9c2.interpretation: The symbol $\Omega(N, q)$ denotes the total microstate multiplicity. The parameter $N$ is the integer number of one-dimensional harmonic oscillators in the crystal lattice. The variable $q$ represents the total number of energy quanta, corresponding to an internal thermal energy of $U = q \hbar \omega$ above the zero-point baseline. The factor $(N - 1)!$ accounts for permutations of the dividers between oscillators, while $q!$ accounts for the indistinguishability of the energy quanta.
multiplicity-identity-1-7bea30c9-053f9c2.symmetry_origin: Permutation symmetry of identical energy quanta (Bose-Einstein type indistinguishability in energy exchange) combined with the spatial distinguishability of localized lattice sites.
multiplicity-identity-1-7bea30c9-053f9c2.limits_and_boundary: In the high-energy (classical) limit where $q \gg N$, Stirling's approximation yields $\Omega \approx \left(\frac{e q}{N}\right)^N$, recovering the Dulong-Petit heat capacity $C_V \approx N k_B$. In the low-temperature limit where $q \ll N$, $\Omega \approx \frac{N^q}{q!}$, leading to an exponentially vanishing heat capacity as $T \to 0$ in accordance with the Third Law of Thermodynamics.

\\Omega.description: Total number of accessible microstates for the given macrostate $(N, q)$

q.description: Total number of discrete energy units shared across all oscillators

multiplicity-identity-1-7bea30c9-053f9c2.conceptual_definition: The multiplicity $\Omega(N, q)$ represents the number of distinguishable ways to distribute $q$ indistinguishable energy quanta (each of energy $\hbar \omega$) among $N$ distinguishable, non-interacting one-dimensional quantum harmonic oscillators. It is derived through standard combinatorics as a multiset coefficient (stars and bars method), providing the statistical basis for the microcanonical entropy $S = k_B \ln \Omega$ of an idealized crystal lattice.
multiplicity-identity-1-7bea30c9-053f9c2.intuitive_summary: Think of partitioning $q$ identical energy balls among $N$ distinct bins; the formula counts all possible configurations of arranging the balls and internal bin dividers in a single row.
multiplicity-identity-1-7bea30c9-053f9c2.description: Calculates the total number of microstates (multiplicity) for an Einstein solid consisting of $N$ independent quantum harmonic oscillators sharing $q$ identical quanta of energy.

probability-density.title: Quantum Mechanical Position Probability Density (Born Rule)
probability-density.conceptual_definition: The probability density $\rho(\mathbf{x}, t)$ represents the probability per unit volume of detecting a particle within an infinitesimal volume element $d^3\mathbf{x}$ centered at position $\mathbf{x}$ at time $t$, given by the modulus squared of the wave function $\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)$.
probability-density.intuitive_summary: In quantum mechanics, particles do not possess definite classical trajectories; instead, the squared amplitude of the complex wave function specifies where the particle is most likely to be observed.
probability-density.interpretation: In the relation $\rho(\mathbf{x}, t) = |\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)|^2$, $\rho(\mathbf{x}, t)$ is the spatial probability density with dimensions of $\text{m}^{-3}$. The position vector $\mathbf{x}$ denotes the coordinates in three-dimensional physical space, and $t$ represents time. The quantity $\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)$ is the complex-valued state vector projected onto the continuous position basis, $\langle \mathbf{x} | \psi(t) \rangle$. The modulus squared $|\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)|^2 = \psi^*(\mathbf{x}, t) \psi(\mathbf{x}, t)$ guarantees that $\rho(\mathbf{x}, t) \ge 0$ everywhere, satisfying the non-negativity axiom of probability distributions.
probability-density.symmetry_origin: Global $U(1)$ gauge invariance of the Schrödinger Lagrangian, which via Noether's theorem leads to the local conservation of probability governed by the continuity equation $\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{j} = 0$.
probability-density.limits_and_boundary: As $|\mathbf{x}| \to \infty$, square-integrability requires $\psi(\mathbf{x}, t) \to 0$, ensuring that $\int_{\mathbb{R}^3} \rho(\mathbf{x}, t) d^3\mathbf{x} = 1$. In the classical limit $\hbar \to 0$, the spatial density tends to a delta distribution $\delta(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_{\text{cl}}(t))$ corresponding to a localized classical point mass.

\\rho.name: Probability density
\\rho.description: Spatial probability density of locating the particle at coordinates (x, t)

\\psi.name: Wave function
\\psi.description: Complex probability amplitude of the quantum state in position space

probability-density.description: Defines the position-space probability density of a non-relativistic quantum particle as the squared modulus of its complex wave function.

gravitational-potential.title: Gravitational Potential of a Point Mass
gravitational-potential.conceptual_definition: The gravitational potential $\Phi$ is a scalar field representing the work required per unit mass to move an object from a defined reference point (conventionally, infinity) to a specific location within a gravitational field. For a spherically symmetric mass $M$, the potential at a distance $r$ is given by $\Phi = -G M / r$. The negative sign indicates that gravity is an attractive force, and the potential energy of a test mass decreases as it approaches the source mass.
gravitational-potential.intuitive_summary: Imagine gravity as creating a 'potential well' in space. The value of the potential $\Phi$ tells you how deep you are in that well. The closer you are to a massive object, the deeper you are (more negative potential), and the more energy is required to climb out to 'flat' space at infinity, where the potential is defined to be zero.
gravitational-potential.interpretation: In the equation $\Phi = -G M / r$, the term $\Phi$ represents the gravitational potential, a scalar quantity measured in Joules per kilogram (J/kg). This potential is generated by a central mass $M$ (in kg) and is evaluated at a radial distance $r$ (in m) from the center of mass. The constant $G$ is the universal gravitational constant, approximately $6.674 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2$, which quantifies the strength of the gravitational interaction. The formula demonstrates that the potential $\Phi$ is inversely proportional to the distance $r$. As $r$ increases, the potential becomes less negative, approaching zero at infinity. Conversely, as $r$ decreases, the potential becomes more negative, signifying a stronger gravitational field and a lower potential energy state.
gravitational-potential.symmetry_origin: The existence of a scalar potential for the gravitational field is a direct consequence of the field being conservative and irrotational ($\nabla \times \mathbf{g} = 0$). This property stems from the central nature of the gravitational force, which is invariant under spatial rotations (isotropy of space), leading to the conservation of angular momentum.
gravitational-potential.limits_and_boundary: In the limit of infinite distance, $r \to \infty$, the potential approaches zero, $\Phi \to 0$, which is the standard reference convention. At the origin for a true point mass, $r \to 0$, the potential diverges to negative infinity, $\Phi \to -\infty$, indicating a singularity. This formula is a non-relativistic, weak-field approximation, valid when the dimensionless potential is small, i.e., $|\Phi|/c^2 \ll 1$.

\\Phi.name: Gravitational Potential
\\Phi.description: The potential energy per unit mass at a specific point in a gravitational field.

G.description: The empirical physical constant quantifying the magnitude of the gravitational force between two bodies.

electromagnetic-four-potential-component.title: Electromagnetic four-potential components
electromagnetic-four-potential-component.conceptual_definition: The formula describes the electromagnetic four-potential, a fundamental object in relativistic electrodynamics that unifies the electric and magnetic fields into a single four-vector. This four-potential is crucial because it is the source from which the electromagnetic field tensor can be derived, and it simplifies Maxwell's equations in a covariant manner.
electromagnetic-four-potential-component.intuitive_summary: The electromagnetic four-potential is a four-vector combining the scalar electric potential and the negative of the magnetic vector potential, adapted for relativistic spacetime.
electromagnetic-four-potential-component.interpretation: The equation defines the electromagnetic four-potential, denoted as a four-vector $A_\mu$. In special relativity, spacetime is treated as a four-dimensional manifold with coordinates $(ct, x, y, z)$, where $c$ is the speed of light and $t$ is time. The four-potential $A_\mu$ is a four-component object. Its first component, $A_0$, is proportional to the scalar electric potential, $\Phi$, divided by the speed of light, $c$. This component is $( \Phi / c )$. The remaining three components, $A_1, A_2, A_3$, form a three-vector $-\mathbf{A}, where \mathbf{A} is the magnetic vector potential. The negative sign in front of \mathbf{A}$ is a convention that ensures the correct relationship with the electromagnetic field tensor. This four-potential is the fundamental quantity from which the electric field $\mathbf{E}$ and magnetic field $\mathbf{B} can be derived: \mathbf{E} = - \nabla \Phi - \frac{\partial \mathbf{A} }{\partial t}$ and $\mathbf{B} = \nabla$ imes $\mathbf{A}$. The use of four-potentials simplifies the formulation of electrodynamics in a Lorentz-covariant way, treating space and time on an equal footing.
electromagnetic-four-potential-component.symmetry_origin: The concept of the four-potential arises from the need to express electromagnetism in a manifestly Lorentz-covariant form. By combining the scalar electric potential and the vector magnetic potential into a single four-vector, Maxwell's equations can be written in a way that is invariant under Lorentz transformations, reflecting the fundamental symmetry of spacetime in special relativity.
electromagnetic-four-potential-component.limits_and_boundary: In the non-relativistic limit (where the speed of phenomena is much less than the speed of light, $v \to 0$), the time-dependent terms involving $c$ in relativistic formulations become less significant. The scalar potential $\Phi$ can be thought of as the primary potential, and the magnetic effects (related to $\mathbf{A}$) become secondary or negligible in scenarios where velocities are very low. Conversely, at extremely high speeds or in relativistic scenarios, both the scalar and vector potentials contribute significantly and are intrinsically linked through the spacetime structure.

normalization-constant-plane-waves.title: Normalization Constant for Three-Dimensional Quantum Plane Waves
normalization-constant-plane-waves.conceptual_definition: In quantum mechanics, continuous momentum eigenstates in the position representation are given by plane waves $\psi_{\mathbf{p}}(\mathbf{r}) = C e^{i \mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{r} / \hbar}$. Setting the normalization constant $C = (2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}$ ensures that the Fourier transform between position space $\psi(\mathbf{r})$ and momentum space $\Phi(\mathbf{p})$ preserves unitarity and satisfies the Dirac delta normalization $\int \psi_{\mathbf{p}'}^*(\mathbf{r}) \psi_{\mathbf{p}}(\mathbf{r}) d^3\mathbf{r} = \delta^{(3)}(\mathbf{p}' - \mathbf{p})$.
normalization-constant-plane-waves.intuitive_summary: Because free particles are not confined to a finite box, their wavefunctions cannot be normalized to unity; instead, they are normalized to a Dirac delta function in momentum space, requiring a factor of $(2\pi\hbar)^{-1/2}$ per spatial dimension.
normalization-constant-plane-waves.interpretation: The constant $C = (2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}$ represents the symmetric Fourier expansion amplitude per state in three-dimensional configuration space. Here, $\hbar$ is the reduced Planck constant (with units $\text{J}\cdot\text{s}$ or $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$), and the factor $2\pi\hbar = h$ represents the fundamental elementary cell size in one-dimensional phase space. The exponent $-3/2$ corresponds to three independent spatial dimensions, rendering the physical units of $C$ as $\text{m}^{-3/2}$, which matches the dimensional requirement for a continuous three-dimensional position wavefunction.
normalization-constant-plane-waves.symmetry_origin: Spatial translation invariance under the continuous abelian group $\mathbb{R}^3$, where momentum $\mathbf{p}$ serves as the generator of translations and yields plane waves as irreducible representations.
normalization-constant-plane-waves.limits_and_boundary: In $d$ spatial dimensions, the constant generalizes to $(2\pi\hbar)^{-d/2}$. When placing the system in a finite volume $V = L^3$ with periodic boundary conditions (box normalization), the continuum constant transitions to the discrete normalization factor $V^{-1/2} = L^{-3/2}$ as the continuous spectrum is discretized.

\\hbar.description: Fundamental quantum of action divided by 2*pi

decay-rate-action-relation.title: Decay Rate of a Metastable Vacuum (Instanton Method)
decay-rate-action-relation.conceptual_definition: The decay rate per unit volume, $\Gamma/V$, of a metastable quantum vacuum is proportional to a non-perturbative factor, $e^{-S_E/\hbar}$. This result is derived from a semi-classical approximation of the path integral in Euclidean spacetime. $S_E$ is the Euclidean action of the 'bounce' solution, a classical solution in imaginary time that represents the most probable tunneling path from the false vacuum to the true vacuum.
decay-rate-action-relation.intuitive_summary: Imagine a ball in a small dip on a hillside. Classically, it's stable. Quantum mechanics allows it to 'tunnel' through the hill to the lower valley. The 'cost' of this tunneling path is the Euclidean action, $S_E$. A higher or wider hill (larger $S_E$) makes tunneling exponentially less likely, leading to a longer lifetime for the 'stuck' state. This formula captures this exponential suppression of the decay probability.
decay-rate-action-relation.interpretation: In this relation, $\Gamma$ is the total decay rate of the metastable state, with units of inverse time ($\text{s}^{-1}$). $V$ is the spatial volume of the system ($\text{m}^3$), making $\Gamma/V$ the decay rate per unit volume. $S_E$ represents the Euclidean action of the 'bounce' or 'instanton' solution that mediates the tunneling; in natural units common to quantum field theory, it is dimensionless. $\hbar$ is the reduced Planck constant ($\text{J} \cdot \text{s}$). The factor $e^{-S_E/\hbar}$ is the dominant suppression term, indicating that transitions with a large action barrier $S_E$ are exponentially improbable.
decay-rate-action-relation.symmetry_origin: This formula is not a direct consequence of a symmetry via Noether's theorem. It is a non-perturbative result derived from the path integral formalism of quantum mechanics, specifically using the semi-classical (instanton) method in Euclidean spacetime to calculate quantum tunneling probabilities.
decay-rate-action-relation.limits_and_boundary: In the classical limit, as $\hbar \to 0$, the ratio $S_E/\hbar \to \infty$, causing the exponential factor $e^{-S_E/\hbar} \to 0$. Consequently, the decay rate $\Gamma \to 0$, correctly reproducing the classical result that a system in a local potential minimum is perfectly stable. The formula is derived under the semi-classical approximation, which is valid when $S_E/\hbar \gg 1$.

null-conformal-factor.title: Degenerate Conformal Factor Condition
null-conformal-factor.conceptual_definition:
In the context of a conformal transformation of a metric tensor $g_{\mu
u}$ to a new metric $\hat{g}_{\mu
u} = \Omega^2(x) g_{\mu
u}$, the condition $\Omega(x) = 0$ defines a degenerate conformal factor. This implies that the resulting metric $\hat{g}_{\mu
u}$ is the zero tensor, causing the spacetime interval $d\hat{s}^2$ to be zero for any displacement $dx^\mu$.
null-conformal-factor.intuitive_summary: Imagine you have a map with a scaling factor that tells you how to convert distances on paper to real-world distances. The condition $\Omega(x) = 0$ is like this scaling factor becoming zero everywhere. Any distance you measure on the map, no matter how large, corresponds to zero actual distance. All points effectively collapse onto a single point.
null-conformal-factor.interpretation:
The equation $\Omega(x) = 0$ specifies that the conformal factor, denoted by the scalar function $\Omega(x)$, is zero at every point $x$ in the manifold or spacetime. In a conformal transformation, the metric tensor $g_{\mu
u}$ is rescaled to a new metric $\hat{g}_{\mu
u}$ via the relation $\hat{g}_{\mu
u}(x) = \Omega^2(x) g_{\mu
u}(x)$. When $\Omega(x) = 0$, the new metric $\hat{g}_{\mu
u}$ becomes the zero tensor. Consequently, the line element $d\hat{s}^2 = \hat{g}_{\mu
u} dx^\mu dx^
u$ becomes zero for any infinitesimal displacement $dx^\mu$. This signifies a complete breakdown of the metric structure, as the notion of distance, length, and angle becomes ill-defined and trivial. All points are, in a metric sense, indistinguishable from one another.
null-conformal-factor.symmetry_origin: This condition represents a singular limit of conformal symmetry (or Weyl symmetry), where the scaling transformation degenerates the entire metric structure of spacetime. It is not associated with a conserved quantity via Noether's theorem but rather a point of catastrophic failure in the geometry.
null-conformal-factor.limits_and_boundary: This is not a limiting case in the usual sense (e.g., $v \to c$), but a specific, singular condition imposed on the conformal factor $\Omega(x)$. If $\Omega(x)$ were a function approaching zero, i.e., $\Omega(x) \to 0$, the geometry would progressively shrink until, at the limit $\Omega(x) = 0$, it becomes completely degenerate. This condition is often avoided in physical theories as it represents a singularity where the theory breaks down.

jacobian-determinant-deformation.title: Jacobian Determinant of the Deformation Gradient
jacobian-determinant-deformation.conceptual_definition: The Jacobian determinant $J = \det(\mathbf{F})$ quantifies the local volumetric dilatation of an infinitesimal continuum element transitioning from a reference Lagrangian configuration $\mathbf{X}$ to a current Eulerian configuration $\mathbf{x}$. It relates the differential volume elements via $dV = J dV_0$ and ensures material impenetrability and orientation preservation through the strict requirement $J > 0$.
jacobian-determinant-deformation.intuitive_summary: It measures how much a tiny chunk of material expands, shrinks, or keeps its volume as the body deforms.
jacobian-determinant-deformation.interpretation: In continuum kinematics, the deformation mapping is given by $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{\Phi}(\mathbf{X}, t)$. The deformation gradient tensor $\mathbf{F} = \nabla_{\mathbf{X}} \mathbf{\Phi}$ describes local stretching and rotation. The scalar $J = \det(\mathbf{F})$ represents the local volume ratio $dV / dV_0$. An isochoric (incompressible) deformation corresponds to $J = 1$, local expansion to $J > 1$, and local compression to $0 < J < 1$. Negative or zero values ($J \le 0$) violate physical non-interpenetration of matter.
jacobian-determinant-deformation.symmetry_origin: Invariance under material frame indifference (principle of objectivity) and proper spatial rotations $\mathrm{SO}(3)$, reflecting local diffeomorphism invariance of physical space.
jacobian-determinant-deformation.limits_and_boundary: In the rigid body limit $\mathbf{F} \in \mathrm{SO}(3)$, $J = 1$. As the material approaches infinite compression, $J \to 0^+$, where strain energy densities typically diverge to prevent self-penetration.

zero-entropy-limit.title: Zero Entropy Limit
zero-entropy-limit.conceptual_definition: The zero entropy limit $S 	o 0$ describes the state of a system whose thermodynamic entropy approaches zero. By Boltzmann's entropy formula $S = k_{\text{B}} \ln \Omega$, this limit implies that the number of accessible microstates $\Omega$ approaches unity ($\,\Omega \to 1\,$), signifying a pure quantum state with zero statistical uncertainty. According to the Nernst Heat Theorem (the Third Law of Thermodynamics), this condition is asymptotically attained as absolute temperature approaches zero ($T \to 0$) for systems in internal thermodynamic equilibrium with non-degenerate ground states.
zero-entropy-limit.intuitive_summary: As a system's entropy approaches zero, all thermal randomness disappears, forcing the system into a single, perfectly ordered microscopic configuration.
zero-entropy-limit.interpretation: The symbol $S$ denotes the thermodynamic or von Neumann entropy of the system. The limit $S \to 0$ corresponds to a transition from a statistical mixed state to a pure state characterized by a density matrix $\rho = |\psi_0\rangle \langle \psi_0|$ with vanishing von Neumann entropy $S = -\operatorname{Tr}(\rho \ln \rho) = 0$. In classical thermodynamics, it marks the baseline reference state for the absolute entropy scale.
zero-entropy-limit.symmetry_origin: Emerges from the fundamental structure of quantum state space and the uniqueness of the vacuum or ground state under Hamiltonian time-translation symmetry.
zero-entropy-limit.limits_and_boundary: In the limit $T \to 0$, $S \to 0$ for regular, non-frustrated systems without ground-state degeneracy. Conversely, in systems exhibiting macroscopic ground-state degeneracy or geometric frustration (such as spin glasses or water ice), a non-zero residual entropy persists as $T \to 0$.

einstein-hilbert-action-gravity.title: Einstein-Hilbert Action (Geometric Core Formulation)
einstein-hilbert-action-gravity.conceptual_definition: The Einstein-Hilbert action represents the integrated spacetime Ricci curvature scalar weighted by the invariant volume element $\sqrt{-g}\,d^4x$. Formulated in normalized or geometric units where $16\pi G / c^4 = 1$, the action $S = \int R \sqrt{-g}\,d^4x$ embodies the principle of stationary action applied to Riemannian/Lorentzian geometry, establishing that the dynamical geometry of spacetime minimizes total integrated spacetime curvature.
einstein-hilbert-action-gravity.intuitive_summary: Spacetime behaves like an elastic manifold whose dynamics are governed by minimizing the total amount of intrinsic curvature over the four-dimensional volume.
einstein-hilbert-action-gravity.interpretation:
The quantity $S$ denotes the total gravitational action. The integrand consists of $R = g^{\mu
u} R_{\mu
u}$, the Ricci scalar invariant formed by contracting the metric tensor $g^{\mu
u}$ with the Ricci curvature tensor $R_{\mu
u}$, quantifying local spacetime curvature. The term $\sqrt{-g}$ represents the square root of the absolute determinant of the metric tensor $g_{\mu
u}$, which compensates for coordinate transformations. The product $\sqrt{-g}\,d^4x$ constitutes the diffeomorphism-invariant four-dimensional volume form on the spacetime manifold $\mathcal{M}$. Setting $\delta S / \delta g^{\mu
u} = 0$ reproduces the source-free Einstein field equations $R_{\mu
u} -  rac{1}{2} R g_{\mu
u} = 0$.
einstein-hilbert-action-gravity.symmetry_origin: General covariance under spacetime diffeomorphisms (smooth coordinate transformations $x^\mu \to x'^\mu$), ensuring invariance under the group $\mathrm{Diff}(\mathcal{M})$.
einstein-hilbert-action-gravity.limits_and_boundary:
In the limit of flat Minkowski spacetime where $g_{\mu
u} 	o \eta_{\mu
u}$, the Riemann tensor vanishes, yielding $R 	o 0$ and $S 	o 0$. In weak-field, slow-motion regimes ($g_{00} \approx -(1 + 2\Phi/c^2)$, $v \ll c$), stationary variation of the action recovers Poisson's equation for Newtonian gravity $
abla^2 \Phi = 4\pi G ho$ upon coupling to matter.

strong-coupling-limit.title: Strong Coupling Limit in Quantum Field Theory
strong-coupling-limit.conceptual_definition: The strong coupling limit describes a physical regime where the dimensionless coupling constant, denoted by $g$, which parameterizes the strength of an interaction in a quantum field theory, approaches infinity ($g \to \infty$). In this limit, the interaction term in the Lagrangian dominates the kinetic term, and standard perturbative expansions in powers of $g$ fail to converge.
strong-coupling-limit.intuitive_summary: Imagine particles connected by springs. In the weak coupling limit, the springs are loose, and particles move almost freely. In the strong coupling limit, the springs are incredibly stiff, binding the particles so tightly that their collective behavior, not their individual motion, defines the system's properties. This is analogous to how quarks are 'glued' together inside protons and neutrons by the strong force.
strong-coupling-limit.interpretation: The equation $g \to \infty$ represents a limit where the coupling constant, denoted by $g$, approaches infinity. The coupling constant $g$ is a fundamental parameter in quantum field theories that quantifies the strength of the interaction between different fields or particles. For instance, in Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), the coupling $g_s$ governs the strength of the strong nuclear force between quarks and gluons. When $g_s$ is large, the interactions are so potent that they dictate the dynamics of the system. This can lead to phenomena like quark confinement, where quarks are never observed as free particles, and instead form bound states called hadrons (like protons and neutrons). The mathematical implication is that standard perturbative techniques, which rely on expanding physical quantities as a power series in $g$ (or its square, $\alpha = g^2/4\pi$), become invalid. New analytical or numerical techniques, such as lattice field theory, AdS/CFT correspondence (holographic duality), or other non-perturbative methods, are necessary to understand systems in this limit.
strong-coupling-limit.symmetry_origin: This limit does not originate from a fundamental symmetry itself, but rather describes a dynamical regime of a theory that possesses an underlying symmetry (e.g., the $SU(3)$ gauge symmetry of Quantum Chromodynamics). The behavior of the system in this limit, such as confinement, is a direct consequence of the non-Abelian nature of that gauge symmetry.
strong-coupling-limit.limits_and_boundary: The strong coupling limit ($g \to \infty$) is the opposite of the weak coupling limit ($g \to 0$), where perturbation theory is applicable. In many non-Abelian gauge theories, such as QCD, the coupling constant $g$ is not fixed but 'runs' with the energy scale $\mu$ (a phenomenon described by the renormalization group). At low energies (large distances), the coupling becomes strong, leading to the strong coupling regime and confinement. Conversely, at high energies (short distances), the coupling becomes weak, a property known as asymptotic freedom.

metric-tensor.title: Spacetime Metric Tensor
metric-tensor.conceptual_definition:
The metric tensor $g_{\mu
u}$ is a non-degenerate, symmetric $(0,2)$-tensor field that establishes an inner product on the tangent space $T_p M$ at each point of a four-dimensional pseudo-Riemannian manifold $M$. It defines the invariant spacetime interval via the quadratic form $ds^2 = g_{\mu
u} dx^\mu dx^
u$, establishes the causal light-cone structure, and serves as the dynamical degree of freedom in General Relativity.
metric-tensor.intuitive_summary: The metric tensor acts as the foundational measuring tool for spacetime, defining local distances, durations of proper time, angles, and the trajectory of free-falling observers.
metric-tensor.interpretation:
In General Relativity, $g_{\mu
u}$ functions as the relativistic gravitational potential. The component $g_{00}$ mediates gravitational time dilation and Newtonian gravitational acceleration in the weak-field limit. The spatial components $g_{ij}$ ($i,j \in \{1,2,3\}$) quantify spatial curvature and length contraction, whereas off-diagonal time-space components $g_{0i}$ quantify gravitomagnetic and frame-dragging effects. The metric and its inverse $g^{\mu
u}$ provide the canonical isomorphism between vectors and dual vectors (index lowering $V_\mu = g_{\mu
u} V^
u$ and index raising $V^\mu = g^{\mu
u} V_
u$), while its determinant $g = \det(g_{\mu
u})$ sets the invariant volume element $d\Omega = \sqrt{-g}\,d^4x$.
metric-tensor.symmetry_origin: General covariance under the spacetime diffeomorphism group $\mathrm{Diff}(M)$ and local Lorentz invariance $\mathrm{SO}(1,3)$ on the tangent bundle.
metric-tensor.limits_and_boundary:
In the limit of vanishing gravitational curvature (Riemann tensor $R^ho{}_{\sigma\mu
u} 	o 0$), $g_{\mu
u}$ reduces everywhere to the flat Minkowski metric $\eta_{\mu
u} = \mathrm{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. For isolated systems at asymptotic infinity ($r 	o \infty$), boundary conditions require $g_{\mu
u} 	o \eta_{\mu
u} + \mathcal{O}(1/r)$.

wavelength-as-observed-by-a-detector-cf7.title: Wavelength as Observed by a Detector
wavelength-as-observed-by-a-detector-cf7.description: Represents the wavelength of an electromagnetic wave measured in the rest frame of an observer or detector, modified from its emitted rest-frame value by kinematic Doppler shifts, gravitational potentials, or cosmological cosmic expansion.
wavelength-as-observed-by-a-detector-cf7.conceptual_definition: The observed wavelength $\lambda_{\text{ob}}$ is the spatial period of electromagnetic radiation measured along null geodesics projected onto the four-velocity $u^\mu_{\text{ob}}$ of an observer's detector at spacetime coordinates $x_{\text{ob}}^\mu$. In cosmological FLRW spacetimes, it scales directly with cosmic expansion via $\lambda_{\text{ob}} = \lambda_{\text{em}} (1 + z) = \lambda_{\text{em}} \frac{a(t_{\text{ob}})}{a(t_{\text{em}})}$.
wavelength-as-observed-by-a-detector-cf7.interpretation: The quantity $\lambda_{\text{ob}}$ denotes the physical wavelength registered at detection time $t_{\text{ob}}$. When compared to the rest-frame emitted wavelength $\lambda_{\text{em}}$, it determines the spectral redshift $z = (\lambda_{\text{ob}} - \lambda_{\text{em}}) / \lambda_{\text{em}}$. In standard cosmological contexts, the ratio $\lambda_{\text{ob}} / \lambda_{\text{em}}$ reflects the ratio of FLRW scale factors $a(t_{\text{ob}})/a(t_{\text{em}})$.
wavelength-as-observed-by-a-detector-cf7.limits_and_boundary: In a static Minkowski spacetime where relative velocity vanishes ($v \to 0$, $a(t) = \text{const}$), $\lambda_{\text{ob}} \to \lambda_{\text{em}}$. For ultra-relativistic receding sources ($v \to c$) or horizons as $a(t_{\text{ob}})/a(t_{\text{em}}) \to \infty$, $\lambda_{\text{ob}} \to \infty$.
wavelength-as-observed-by-a-detector-cf7.symmetry_origin: Diffeomorphism invariance of general relativity and conformal invariance of Maxwell's equations in curved spacetime along null geodesics.

wavelength-as-observed-by-a-detector-cf7.intuitive_summary: As photons travel across expanding space or relative velocity fields to reach an observer's instrument, their physical wavelengths stretch or compress, defining the measured wavelength $\lambda_{\text{ob}}$.

elementary-charge-constant-value-b5c9a16.title: Numerical Value of the Elementary Charge
elementary-charge-constant-value-b5c9a16.description: Represents the fundamental physical constant quantifying the elementary quantum of electric charge, exactly fixed in the SI system as $1.602176634 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.
elementary-charge-constant-value-b5c9a16.conceptual_definition: The elementary charge $e$ is the fundamental unit of electric charge carried by a single proton, or equivalently the negative magnitude of the charge carried by a single electron. Since the 2019 redefinition of SI base units, $e$ is an exactly defined fundamental defining constant ($e = 1.602176634 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$), which serves to define the SI unit of electric current, the ampere, via $\text{A} = \text{C}/\text{s}$.
elementary-charge-constant-value-b5c9a16.interpretation: The constant $e \approx 1.602 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ dictates the coupling scale of the electromagnetic interaction. Any isolated observable charge $Q$ is quantized according to $Q = n e$, where $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ for all asymptotic unconfined states. In quantum electrodynamics, $e$ is related to the fine-structure constant $\alpha$ via $\alpha = \frac{e^2}{4\pi \varepsilon_0 \hbar c}$.
elementary-charge-constant-value-b5c9a16.limits_and_boundary: In high-energy quantum field theory, the effective running coupling $e(\mu)$ increases logarithmically with energy scale $\mu$ due to vacuum polarization screening, approaching a Landau pole at non-perturbatively high energies.
elementary-charge-constant-value-b5c9a16.symmetry_origin: Charge quantization and conservation arise from the global and local $U(1)$ gauge invariance of the electromagnetic action via Noether's theorem.

virial-coefficient-for-quadratic-potenti.title: Virial Exponent for Quadratic Potentials
virial-coefficient-for-quadratic-potenti.description: Defines the degree of homogeneity $k = 2$ for harmonic or quadratic potential energy functions within the generalized virial theorem.
virial-coefficient-for-quadratic-potenti.conceptual_definition: In classical and quantum mechanics, Euler's homogeneous function theorem implies that for a potential function satisfying $V(\lambda \mathbf{r}) = \lambda^k V(\mathbf{r})$, the time-averaged or expectation-value virial relation takes the form $2\langle T \rangle = k \langle V \rangle$. For quadratic potentials (e.g., simple harmonic oscillators) where $V(r) \propto r^2$, the degree of homogeneity is explicitly $k = 2$, yielding the equipartition of time-averaged kinetic and potential energies $\langle T \rangle = \langle V \rangle$.
virial-coefficient-for-quadratic-potenti.interpretation: The parameter $k$ represents the degree of homogeneity (power-law exponent) of the potential $V(\mathbf{r})$. When $k = 2$, substituting into the virial theorem $2\langle T \rangle = k\langle V \rangle$ yields $2\langle T \rangle = 2\langle V \rangle$, or $\langle T \rangle = \langle V \rangle$. This exact equality between time-averaged kinetic energy $\langle T \rangle$ and potential energy $\langle V \rangle$ is a hallmark of linear restoring forces and harmonic oscillations.
virial-coefficient-for-quadratic-potenti.limits_and_boundary: In the limit of small displacements about a stable potential minimum ($x \to 0$), any smooth potential $V(x)$ expands via Taylor series as $V(x) \approx V(0) + \frac{1}{2} V''(0) x^2$, making $k = 2$ the universal effective exponent for small-amplitude linear oscillations. For large amplitudes where anharmonic terms become non-negligible, the effective degree $k$ deviates from 2.
virial-coefficient-for-quadratic-potenti.symmetry_origin: Continuous scale invariance / dilation symmetry of the action under coordinate rescalings $r \to \lambda r$ combined with time rescalings $t \to \lambda^{1 - k/2} t$. For $k = 2$, time scales linearly with spatial dilation ($t \to t$), leading to isochronous orbits (period independent of amplitude).

k.name: degree of homogeneity
k.description: Homogeneity exponent of the potential function $V(\mathbf{r}) \propto r^k$, equal to 2 for quadratic/harmonic potentials.

virial-coefficient-for-quadratic-potenti.intuitive_summary: For a standard harmonic oscillator or spring-like potential, the energy scales quadratically with distance. Consequently, the virial coefficient is 2, ensuring that on average, energy is shared equally between kinetic motion and potential storage.

lepton-number-for-a-particle-state-ab3c8.title: Lepton Quantum Number for a Single-Particle State
lepton-number-for-a-particle-state-ab3c8.description: Defines the discrete lepton quantum number $n_l$ assigned to a fundamental or composite particle state $l$, characterizing its leptonic charge.
lepton-number-for-a-particle-state-ab3c8.conceptual_definition:
The lepton number $n_l$ is an additive discrete quantum number assigned to individual particle species and states. By convention, standard Model leptons ($e^-$, $\mu^-$, $	au^-$, and their corresponding neutrinos $
u_e, 
u_\mu, 
u_	au$) carry $n_l = +1$, their antipartners carry $n_l = -1$, and non-leptonic states (quarks, hadrons, gauge bosons) carry $n_l = 0$.
lepton-number-for-a-particle-state-ab3c8.interpretation: For any given single-particle quantum state labeled by index $l$, the value $n_l$ acts as the eigenvalue of the single-particle lepton charge operator. In particle interactions, the total lepton number $L = \sum_l N_l n_l$ (where $N_l$ is the state occupation number) remains perturbatively conserved under Standard Model gauge interactions.
lepton-number-for-a-particle-state-ab3c8.limits_and_boundary: In the Standard Model at tree and loop level, $\Delta L = 0$. In Beyond Standard Model scenarios, such as Majorana neutrino mass generation via the Seesaw Mechanism or Grand Unified Theories (GUTs), $n_l$ conservation can be violated with $\Delta L = \pm 2$ (e.g., in neutrinoless double beta decay) or $\Delta L = \pm 1$ (e.g., in proton decay).
lepton-number-for-a-particle-state-ab3c8.symmetry_origin: Associated via Noether's theorem with the global accidental $U(1)_L$ phase invariance of the Standard Model Lagrangian, which is conserved perturbatively but broken non-perturbatively by electroweak sphalerons (conserving $B - L$).
